stances.claim: President Duterte's appointment of Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier during Women's Month -- following his November 2018 appointment of Justice Carandang -- constitutes a rousing tribute to women jurists, intentionally or unintentionally, and the resulting Javier-Carandang-Perlas-Bernabe triumvirate represents top graduates of the three premier PH law schools who 'can match the gravitas of the gentlemen in the Court.'

Javier's and Carandang's path through the 'biblical eye of the needle' -- each requiring eight JBC nominations before SC appointment despite outstanding CA records -- illustrates the unusually high barrier women jurists must clear, even when their substantive qualifications match or exceed those of their male counterparts.
stances.rhetorical_move: biblical-metaphor barrier-quantification (the eye-of-the-needle imagery applied to JBC repeat nominations)

stances.claim: The three women justices must not be expected to vote uniformly -- Bernabe voted for the Marcos LNMB burial while Carandang and Javier publicly disagreed during their JBC interviews -- and this internal independence is a feature, not a bug, of their judicial integrity.

Law school representation in the women's SC contingent is starkly uneven: UP has produced 11 women SC justices, UST has produced 2 (Javier and Sandoval-Gutierrez), and Ateneo has produced only 1 (Bernabe) -- and this distribution does not reflect the institutional age or prestige of these schools.

notable_anecdotes: Carpio besting Carandang in their 1975 UP law class -- Carpio as valedictorian and 6th in the bar (Carandang salutatorian and 9th) -- a class hierarchy that Carandang has now inverted in seniority terms by joining the same Court that Carpio leads as Senior Justice, with Carpio about to retire and Carandang remaining.
Javier and Carandang each surviving 'eight JBC nominations' before finally being appointed -- the most specific quantification of the barrier women jurists must clear in any of CJ's tribute columns.

The 400-year-old UST having produced only 2 women SC justices (Javier and Sandoval-Gutierrez) compared with the 108-year-old UP's 11 -- making institutional age inversely correlated with women's representation in the SC pipeline.
Javier's zero CA backlog over 12 years -- the most institutionally important credential CJ flags, since it directly addresses the SC's own backlog crisis covered in adjacent columns (A248).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban interprets President Duterte's March 2019 (Women's Month) appointment of Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier -- UST magna cum laude valedictorian of the law class of 1982, 12 years on the Court of Appeals with zero backlog, 24 years at the Office of the Solicitor General -- as a 'rousing tribute to women jurists,' following his November 2018 appointment of Justice Rosmari D. Carandang (UP salutatorian of the law class of 1975, ninth-placer in that year's bar exam where she was bested only by Antonio Carpio). Both women required eight JBC nominations apiece -- what CJ calls 'the biblical eye of the needle' -- before finally reaching the Court. Together with incumbent Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe (Ateneo 1976 salutatorian), they form a triumvirate that 'can match the gravitas of the gentlemen in the Court,' though their independence shows in voting divergences (Bernabe favored the Marcos LNMB burial; Carandang and Javier publicly said they would have joined the minority). He notes the striking institutional imbalance: UP has produced 11 women SC justices, UST only 2 (Javier and Sandoval-Gutierrez), and Ateneo only 1 (Bernabe), despite the inverse correlation with each school's institutional age. He closes with the slate of JBC renominees and new entrants competing for the Tijam vacancy -- mostly from the CA, Sandiganbayan, and CTA -- confirming Duterte's documented fondness for appellate-jurist appointments.
